title: The Destruction of the Pocket
subtitle: Fragmented resistance, escape and the passage into German captivity
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: The destruction of the Southwestern Front left survivors scattered, escaping or captive. The study distinguishes prisoner claims from other losses and examines the institutions and choices that made German custody lethal.
body:
A battle ending in different places

By 26 September 1941, German commanders claimed the great pocket east of Kiev had been reduced. Soviet headquarters had been destroyed or dispersed, formations had fragmented, and huge numbers of men were prisoners. Fighting and danger did not end at one moment for everyone. Some soldiers still sought routes east; wounded men might be unable to move; captured survivors entered a system governed by discriminatory German orders. Following the victory means following that passage from military defeat into custody, deprivation and killing.[1][2]a

The decisive change since 16 September was the loss of the ability to act together. Closing the German pincers had interrupted routes. Subsequent attacks divided the space inside them, captured crossings and deprived Soviet formations of the means to coordinate their efforts. The fall of Kiev on 19 September removed the city from Soviet control, but it neither produced a simultaneous surrender farther east nor released every German formation for its next operation. Reducing the pocket required another sequence of movements, engagements and decisions.

Reduction tied German formations to the pocket after the pincers had joined. Mobile troops guarded roads against breakouts; infantry advanced into the enclosed area and took prisoners. Those duties required ammunition, supplies and time that could not also be spent preparing the same troops for the next offensive. The operational result was therefore achieved over successive days. Its cost cannot be read from the moment of contact alone, any more than the number trapped on that date can be treated as a final prisoner count.

For the Soviet side, the collapse of command magnified material inferiority. Men who still possessed weapons might lack ammunition for prolonged resistance, a reliable route east or knowledge of where neighbouring formations stood. Their continued fighting demonstrates that the defeat cannot be reduced to an absence of courage. It also cannot reverse the operational result. An army survives as an army through communications, supply and coordinated movement as well as through the willingness of individuals to resist. Around Kiev, those connecting institutions were being destroyed faster than they could be restored.

The ring becomes a series of smaller battles

The original encirclement contained the 5th, 21st, 26th and 37th Armies, or substantial portions of them, together with other troops and rear services. They had entered the crisis from different positions. The 37th Army had been defending Kiev; the 5th and 21st were associated with the threatened northern sector; the 26th held positions farther south. A withdrawal towards the east therefore began from several fronts and required convergence on roads and crossings already threatened by German mobile formations. It was never a single column marching towards one open gate.[3]

On the German side, Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group continued to face in two directions. Its inner front helped contain the trapped troops; its outer front resisted Soviet forces still operating beyond the pocket. In his postwar study for the U.S. Army, Guderian described the 3rd Panzer Division pushing towards Pyriatyn and the SS Division Das Reich taking Pryluky. These movements tightened the northeastern part of the encirclement by taking places through which Soviet troops might otherwise move. Their significance lay in the roads and communications they controlled, rather than in the addition of two names to a list of captured towns.[2]

The 25th Motorised Infantry Division, approaching from Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group, helped establish the connection with the northern forces and faced Soviet attempts to break through farther south. The infantry armies pressed from the wider perimeter: Weichs’s 2nd Army from the northern side and Reichenau’s 6th Army from the west, while the southern German grouping secured the approaches opened from the Kremenchuk bridgehead. The relationship between the advancing infantry and the mobile formations was crucial. Infantry pressure compressed the Soviet groups; mobile forces could intercept their movement towards the eastern exits. Neither function alone explains the result.[2][1]b

Movement within the pocket became increasingly difficult because the same streams and rivers crossed during the advance now constrained escape. The Udai and Sula systems divided routes into a limited number of usable passages. A formation reaching a crossing could find another group already there, German troops beyond it or no information about the road ahead. Such conditions favoured smaller parties that could abandon vehicles, but they imposed severe disadvantages on artillery, medical units and transport columns. Saving people and saving an organised army were becoming different problems.

German pressure also separated Soviet commanders from the troops they were meant to direct. The published Soviet command conversations record the loss of communications with army headquarters before the fighting ended. On 19 September, higher headquarters were still trying to establish what had happened to the 5th Army after receiving an intercepted appeal from the Pyriatyn area. A missing report was not proof that a formation had surrendered; it was evidence that the command system could no longer dependably locate and employ it. The resulting uncertainty made a coordinated breakout progressively less achievable.[4]c

Headquarters on the road

The Southwestern Front headquarters itself became part of the retreat. Kirponos and his staff could no longer direct the battle from a secure centre connected to the armies by dependable communications. The headquarters column had to move through the same contested countryside as the troops whose movements it was attempting to organise. Its escorts and vehicles offered some protection and mobility, but the concentration also made it a target. The defeat of a headquarters in these circumstances was both a human disaster and the destruction of an institution containing knowledge, records and established working relationships.

Kirponos died in combat on 20 September near the Shumeikove grove by Driukivshchyna, southwest of Lokhvytsia. The Ukrainian academic biographical entry gives that date, while the account of the wider operation places the destruction of the combined front and 5th Army headquarters column across 20–22 September. The column’s fighting continued after his death. Tupikov, the front’s chief of staff, and military council member Burmistenko also died in the command group’s destruction; the wounded 5th Army commander Potapov was captured. These individual outcomes should not be compressed into a single simultaneous event.[5][3]

The loss of the staff was especially damaging because it removed people capable of reconnecting scattered formations. A surviving commander could assemble men locally, but might not know where to find another army’s remnants or where friendly forces beyond the ring could assist. The destruction of radio equipment, codes and transport further narrowed what authority could accomplish. The personal rank of a general remained recognisable; the practical means of exercising command could disappear. That distinction helps explain why survival by individual officers did not mean the Southwestern Front had escaped intact.

The failed communications already examined in The Fall of Kiev constrained assistance from outside. The 20 September discussion of fuel and ammunition deliveries by air establishes an effort to help the encircled troops; it does not document a dependable air bridge. Supplies also needed recipients able to collect and distribute them. A successful delivery might prolong one group’s resistance without restoring contact with another. The loss of headquarters and transport meant that even resources brought into the pocket could no longer be assumed to serve a coordinated breakout. [4]d

Breakout attempts consequently had different outcomes at different scales. A party reaching Soviet lines could preserve trained men and valuable information. A larger formation might force a temporary passage yet lose cohesion during the movement beyond it. Others found their route blocked and fought until their capacity to continue was exhausted. Recognising those differences gives the surviving troops their due without confusing escape with an operational rescue. The central fact remained that the Soviet command could no longer extract the encircled armies as functioning formations.

The outer front still demands fuel

While the trapped forces were being reduced, Soviet attacks outside the encirclement continued to occupy German troops. Guderian’s account places a serious attack near his headquarters at Romny on 18 September, involving Soviet cavalry and tanks. German infantry, antiaircraft weapons employed against ground targets, armour and air support were brought into the response. The episode demonstrates how close an apparent victory could remain to an active threat. A headquarters positioned to control the encirclement was still vulnerable to enemy forces that had never entered it.[2]

On 19 September, Guderian reported that a shortage of fuel restricted the forces he could move eastward: only small elements of Das Reich and the 4th Panzer Division could initially be shifted. The following day, movements from Romny towards Nedryhailiv and from the Putivl area towards Vorozhba sought to push the outer front away from the encirclement. These were efforts to improve security and freedom of movement, not evidence that the Soviet armies outside the pocket had ceased to matter. The Germans had to spend fuel to obtain the space within which they could finish their victory.[2]

Soviet records provide a useful view from the opposite side of this outer battle. The command conversation of 20 September placed Belov’s 9th and 5th Cavalry Divisions east and southeast of Romny after difficult fighting on the previous day. It also reported the 1st Tank Brigade unloading at Lebedyn and concentrating farther west, while the 129th Tank Brigade was gathering closer to Romny. This was a force being assembled through distinct stages, with cavalry already fighting while additional armour arrived by rail. The report explicitly lacked the latest positions of some units. It consequently supports an account of continuing pressure and reinforcement, rather than a claim that every formation was simultaneously ready to attack. The same sequence explains why a German commander might face a serious local threat without facing a fully coordinated Soviet relief offensive. [4]

Soviet attacks around Glukhov also threatened German communications, drawing the 17th Panzer Division into relief of the garrison on 23 September. Forces enforcing the Kiev encirclement still had to send detachments outward, hold back units short of supplies and restore threatened connections. A division’s continued appearance in an order of battle said little about how much strength it could provide for the next offensive while these duties continued.[2]e

German material weakness should therefore be dated and defined. The U.S. Army’s study of the campaign reports that on 4 September only 47 percent of the tanks on the Eastern Front were operational, with another 23 percent in repair and 30 percent disabled. Those figures describe the theatre at an earlier date; they are not a measured inventory of the divisions around Kiev on 26 September. Their value is to establish the deteriorating equipment position in which the final battle developed. A repaired tank could return to service, while a vehicle still counted in a unit’s holdings might be unavailable for its next movement.[6]f

Infantry victory carried its own burden. Marching troops needed food and ammunition, horses needed fodder, and wounded men needed transport back through roads also used for supply. Captured guns and vehicles had to be identified, collected and moved before they became useful resources. Prisoners required guards and provisions. The German command could choose to subordinate those needs to preparation for another offensive, but that choice did not abolish them. In the case of prisoners, the decisions made about supply and movement would become matters of life and death.

Counting a destroyed front

The familiar German claim of 665,000 prisoners expresses the scale of the Kiev victory, but it is not a simple census of men surrendering in one place on 26 September. It was a claim associated with the completed operation. The U.S. Army’s later synthesis places it alongside a Soviet published figure of 677,085 men in the Southwestern Front at the beginning of the battle and 150,541 at its end. These numbers belong to different accounting systems. Subtracting the latter two does not produce a verified prisoner total, because losses, transfers, arrivals, wounded personnel and the boundaries of the reporting period affect the comparison.[1]

Historian Dieter Pohl identifies a broader difficulty in reconciling German capture statistics with Soviet military losses. German prisoner categories could include people outside the Red Army’s regular strength returns, including other uniformed personnel and civilians mobilised for construction or militia service. Soviet reporting also suffered from the collapse of formations and incomplete records. Pohl therefore treats the discrepancy as an unresolved historical accounting problem rather than a reason to accept either series automatically. His discussion makes the figure of roughly 660,000 a German claim requiring definition, not a substitute for tracing who was actually captured.[7]g

Equipment claims require the same care. A gun found abandoned, a tank knocked out and a vehicle subsequently repaired describe different events. German collection reports were measuring the apparent destruction of enemy resources; Soviet loss returns addressed changes within their own organisations. Neither category alone measures how much additional fighting power the German army acquired. A captured weapon without compatible ammunition, trained users or transport might remain a trophy rather than an immediately useful asset. Operational success and usable replenishment were related, but they were not identical.

Behind every loss category was an unresolved individual fate. A man absent from his unit might have been captured, killed, cut off or trying to return. A capture report establishes custody, not his motive; a missing-person entry does not establish desertion. The punitive categories examined in The Kiev Trap cannot fill the gaps in a particular case. Families might still be waiting for information after headquarters had written off the formation.

The disputed totals do not make the scale of defeat uncertain. Several Soviet armies had lost the ability to operate as organised formations, major staffs had been destroyed, and further territory was exposed. Movement reports and command exchanges document that collapse independently of the German prisoner claim. Retaining the distinction between a reported total and the people it counted makes the defeat more intelligible without reducing its magnitude.

The road into captivity

Men reached captivity carrying the exhaustion, hunger and wounds of the battle. Separation from their formations had already broken the systems that fed them, recorded their whereabouts and moved their casualties. German military authorities now controlled access to food, shelter and transport. What happened after surrender depended on those authorities’ policies and choices, as well as on the prisoners’ condition when they were taken.

Pohl distinguishes army collection points, transit camps known as Dulags, and more permanent camps called Stalags. Transfer between them did not remove military responsibility: even camps inside the civilian Reichskommissariat Ukraine remained under Wehrmacht supervision. This institutional chain connected the troops taking prisoners with the authorities responsible for their longer confinement.[7]

The German high command had already defined Soviet captivity in ideological terms. Regulations of 8 September treated Red Army prisoners as bearers of Bolshevism and authorised exceptional severity. They provided for the separation of prisoners classified as politically undesirable and their transfer to Security Police and Security Service units. The military custody system and the security apparatus were connected by policy. A soldier who survived surrender could consequently face further selection and killing after leaving the battlefield.[8]h

A warning read and rejected

On 15 September, Canaris warned Keitel that the prescribed treatment of Soviet prisoners abandoned established protections and could lead to arbitrary killing. Keitel annotated the memorandum on 23 September, sustaining the measures on ideological grounds. Preserved as Nuremberg document EC-338, the exchange identifies an objection reaching the leadership while the Kiev pocket was being destroyed—and a decision to reject it. Canaris’s intervention does not clear the wider military institution of responsibility. It shows that the danger had been raised within that institution and the policy knowingly upheld.[8]i

The treatment of prisoners also exposes the limits of explaining every German failure through insufficient transport. A February 1942 memorandum from Rosenberg’s ministry, preserved as document 081-PS, described guards shooting prisoners unable to keep up on marches and camp commanders preventing civilians from providing food. It also reported a failure to provide shelter or even tools with which prisoners could dig protection. This was a later assessment of the wider system, not an eyewitness report of every Kiev column. Nevertheless, it demonstrates that deprivation involved deliberate restrictions as well as shortage. Food offered by civilians could be available and still be denied.[9]

The memorandum’s purpose was itself revealing. Rosenberg’s ministry wanted to improve recruitment, propaganda and the exploitation of labour. Its criticism did not amount to a rejection of German domination. By describing brutal treatment as a cause of Soviet resistance and a loss to Germany’s economy, it evaluated victims partly through their usefulness to the occupier. The document is powerful evidence against claims that the catastrophe was unknown within the regime, but its proposed remedy remained embedded in the regime’s purposes. Reading it critically requires attention both to the abuses it acknowledged and to the interests behind the complaint.[9]j

A prisoner is more than a number

The attempted assistance recorded in the memorandum deserves attention in its own right. Civilians offered food to prisoners whom the custodial system was failing to feed, and German guards sometimes prevented the exchange. This establishes available help being obstructed; it does not tell us the relationship between every giver and recipient. The act itself is enough to reveal a choice. Outside military authority, inhabitants could try to sustain captured men. Inside that authority, guards could enforce a barrier even when food was close enough to hand over. Captivity’s lethality cannot be explained by transport shortages alone. [9]

Volodymyr Davydov’s route west

Volodymyr Davydov was captured near Pereiaslav in late September. The Ukrainian war museum’s biographical account traces confinement through Pereiaslav, Boryspil, Darnytsia, Kiev and Zhytomyr, followed by escape from the Zhytomyr camp in late October and a return to Kiev. The biographical account does not date every transfer; the accompanying seven-page testimony is a separate source. His route makes a prisoner total tangible as a movement through places and institutions. Escape ended his captivity while leaving him in German-occupied territory; it did not make the system less dangerous for those still held.[10]k

Davydov’s itinerary also shows why a tally at one camp cannot be read as the entire population captured in the battle. Prisoners moved between collection points and camps; some escaped, some were released under particular policies, and others died before a later registration. A total for an institution at a particular date measures those present within its administrative reach. It cannot recover every person who passed through or disappeared along the way. The missing connections between military capture records and later camp records are part of the history, not an invitation to replace evidence with a single dramatic estimate.

Nor can the social consequences be confined to soldiers. The destruction of the Southwestern Front removed an armed barrier between civilians and occupation. Homes, farms and roads became resources for the victors, while people who helped fugitives or prisoners had to judge the new risks of doing so. Jewish soldiers and civilians faced the additional danger created by Nazi racial policy. The Soviet defeat and German decisions about treatment were separate causes operating together: military capture placed people in German power, and the occupiers determined what they would do with that power.[8]

What the victory made possible

By 26 September, Germany had prevented much of the Southwestern Front from escaping as an organised force and opened the way to further operations. It had also assumed custody of prisoners whose treatment was governed by discriminatory orders consciously upheld at the top. These were both consequences of the victory. The formations preparing to move again still carried the summer’s losses and mechanical wear. The U.S. Army campaign study records estimates of several weeks for a proper refit, far more time than the next offensive’s schedule allowed. [6]l

The Soviet state had lost armies, yet troops outside the pocket continued to fight and new forces were being assembled. Germany faced another campaign. For the prisoners, the immediate future depended on guards, food, shelter and the chance of escape, rather than on whether the next German offensive succeeded. The final study, Victory and Catastrophe, brings the military assessment together with the occupation authorities’ preparations to murder Kiev’s Jews.

Retrospective accounts, translated extracts and abstracts are identified where used. Later events retain their own dates. The dated atlas has separate feature sources and precision notes.
